solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Rather weak medic getting very cold with November gone

parts.note: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor, a medic

indicators.note: gone says a letter goes missing from the word for very cold

parts.note: nippy weather is bitingly cold
N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A doctor who feels feeble after catching a chill as November ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Drippy is informal for feeble, wet or ineffectual, so rather weak in character.

clue.text: Volatile dictator's denying first signs of this oppression? That's extreme

indicators.note: volatile means unstable and explosive, so the letters of the clue word are thrown into a new order
first signs of picks the opening letter of each of the two following words

explanation.surface: A tyrant's denial of any oppression, met with the retort that such a claim is extreme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'denying' says that T and O, the first letters of 'this oppression', are taken out of DICTATORS before the rest is rearranged into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Drastic measures are severe or radical ones, so the word is a synonym for extreme.

clue.text: Leader of industry taken on dodgy tour with two MPs? It's not preplanned

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter
dodgy means dubious or unsound, signalling that these letters are rearranged

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament, so two of them give the abbreviation twice

explanation.surface: A captain of industry is taken on a dubious trip with a couple of politicians, all arranged on a whim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken on' puts the I first; the anagram of TOUR with MPMP gives MPROMPTU.
explanation.definitionFit: Something impromptu is done on the spur of the moment, without rehearsal or advance arrangement.

clue.text: Ingredient in apple or other fruit lacking a hard container

indicators.note: lacking says the following letters are taken out of the fruit

parts.note: a peach is a fruit
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard
a tin is a container

explanation.surface: A recipe note about something found in apples or another fruit that has no tough casing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fruit' does double work in the surface but in the parse it is PEACH; removing A and H leaves PEC.
explanation.definitionFit: Pectin is the natural setting agent found in apples and many other fruits, used to make jam set.

clue.text: Get angry with Indian cricketer showing disrespectful levity

parts.note: to flip is to lose your temper
Rishabh Pant is an Indian wicketkeeper-batsman

explanation.surface: A batsman losing his temper and being cheeky about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishabh Pant is a well-known Indian Test cricketer.
explanation.definitionFit: Flippant describes a lack of proper seriousness, treating weighty matters with mocking lightness.

clue.text: Play a prank in large rescue vessel

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
Noah's ark saved the animals from the flood

explanation.surface: Someone fooling about aboard a big lifeboat.
explanation.definitionFit: To lark about is to fool around or play a mischievous trick.

clue.text: First person in Germany probing broadcast tapes in a jumble

indicators.note: probing means poking into, so one piece goes inside the other
broadcast means scattered widely, so these letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: ich is German for I, the first-person pronoun

explanation.surface: A German investigator examining a pile of muddled recordings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person in Germany' is the German word for I; 'broadcast' rearranges TAPES so that it can be prised open after its fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastiche can be a medley or hotchpotch of borrowed bits, so a jumble of elements.

clue.text: Light stroll or walk in the countryside skirting river

indicators.note: skirting means going round and so avoiding, so the river's letter is left out

parts.note: a ramble is a country walk

explanation.surface: A gentle walk across fields that keeps to the riverbank.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a slow, relaxed pace, so an amble is an easy saunter.

clue.text: Carer mistakenly enters vacant theatre in a row of houses

indicators.note: enters means goes inside, so the rearranged letters sit within the emptied word
vacant means emptied, keeping only the outer letters of the word
mistakenly signals the letters are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A care worker wanders by mistake into an empty playhouse on a residential street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vacant' empties theatre to its outer letters, and 'mistakenly' scrambles CARER into ERRAC to fill the gap; 'in a' only links the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrace is a line of joined houses built in a continuous block, common in British towns.

clue.text: Feature of city in past in a ruined state

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other
a ruined state means wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: EC is the postcode for the City of London

explanation.surface: A detail of a town as it once was, now lying in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'city' is the City of London, whose postcode EC is a crossword staple; 'in a ruined state' gives ASPT.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspect is a particular part or facet of something, so a feature of it.

clue.text: A hybrid drinking haunt? It's supported by posts

parts.note: a cross is a hybrid of two breeds or varieties
a bar is a place to drink

explanation.surface: A pub that is half one thing and half another, propped up by its regulars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'posts' suggests mail or regulars, but it means goalposts, which hold up the bar between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossbar is the horizontal beam resting on two goalposts or rugby uprights.

clue.text: Illness sadly besetting island in the Middle East

indicators.note: in places the combined piece within the two letters of the region

parts.note: ME is the abbreviation for the Middle East

indicators.note: besetting means surrounding on all sides, so one piece is wrapped round the other

parts.note: alas is said sadly, an expression of grief
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Someone falls unhappily sick on an island somewhere in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'besetting' wraps ALAS round I to give ALAIS, which 'in' places between M and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaise is a general feeling of unease or bodily discomfort, a vague sickness.

clue.text: Very warm current found around centre of Mediterranean

indicators.note: found around means placed so as to surround, so the outer word encloses the picked letter

parts.note: topical means of current interest

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A warm sea current found circling the middle of the Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current' looks like a sea current but it is the adjective, meaning up to date.
explanation.definitionFit: Tropical weather is hot and humid, like conditions near the equator.

clue.text: Place for screening agents covering males from the east

indicators.note: covering means wrapping over, so the agency's letters enclose the other piece

parts.note: the CIA is the American intelligence agency, a body of agents

indicators.note: from the east means read right to left, as an across clue's west is its start

parts.note: men are males

explanation.surface: Spies shielding men arriving from the east, a security screening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the east' turns MEN into NEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A cinema is a building where films are shown on a screen to an audience.

clue.text: Writer and poet clipped hanging item

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

indicators.note: clipped means trimmed, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: Dante is the Italian poet of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: An author and a poet both cut short, with something dangling.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendant is a piece of jewellery suspended from a chain, so something that dangles.

clue.text: Imitate something supplied by journalists

definitions.meaning: the written material a reporter files for publication

explanation.surface: Press reporters accused of plagiarism.
explanation.definitionFit: Copy means both to reproduce and, in journalism, the text a writer submits.

clue.text: Escort person in custody and assume control

parts.note: to take someone somewhere is to escort them
a charge is someone in your care or keeping

explanation.surface: A guard leads a prisoner away and takes over.
explanation.definitionFit: To take charge is to assume command or responsibility.

clue.text: Artist beginning to consider much of new tour possibly as a fund of stories

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter
possibly means the letters might be arranged some other way
much of means most of the word, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A painter starts weighing up most of a new trip as material for anecdotes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'much of' drops W from NEW; 'possibly' turns NE plus TOUR into ONTEUR.
explanation.definitionFit: A raconteur is a person who tells anecdotes skilfully, someone full of tales.

clue.text: A charm proving deceptive in case of phoney source of drugs

indicators.note: in puts the rearranged letters inside the outer pair
the case of a word is its outside, the first and last letters
proving deceptive suggests letters that are not what they seem, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A charm that turns out to be fake inside a phoney's casing, as a supply of dodgy medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'proving deceptive' turns A CHARM into HARMAC, which sits inside the P and Y of 'case of phoney'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharmacy is a chemist's shop that dispenses medicines.

clue.text: Disregard president holding Republican ideas wrongly

indicators.note: holding means containing, so one letter is gripped inside the name

parts.note: George Bush, father or son, was a US president

indicators.note: wrongly means the letters are in an incorrect order

explanation.surface: A president harbouring a Republican's mistaken notions.
explanation.definitionFit: To brush aside is to dismiss or ignore something without considering it.

clue.text: Cry over old American that's become bloated

indicators.note: over in a down clue means turned upside down, read from the bottom

parts.note: to blub is to weep

explanation.surface: Weeping about an elderly American who has put on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns BLUB into BULB.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulbous means round and swollen, like a bulb, so puffed up.

clue.text: What a pack might do, being heartless, worthless types?

indicators.note: heartless means losing the central letter

parts.note: a rugby pack forms a scrum

explanation.surface: A pack of hounds behaving cruelly, as no-good people do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pack' suggests wolves or cards, but it is the rugby forwards, who scrum down.
explanation.definitionFit: Scum is a contemptuous term for people regarded as despicable or of no value.

clue.text: Friend keeps revolutionary tool used by workers in fields?

definitions.text: tool used by workers in fields?

indicators.note: keeps means holds within, so the friend's letters enclose the other piece

parts.note: a mate is a friend
Che Guevara was the Latin American revolutionary

explanation.surface: A pal holding on to a revolutionary farm implement.
explanation.definitionFit: A machete is a broad blade used to cut cane and vegetation in plantations.

clue.text: Sun is seen above clear herbaceous plant

indicators.note: in a down clue, above means placed earlier in the answer

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for Sunday
to purge is to clear out

explanation.surface: Sunshine falling above a cleared bed of plants.
explanation.walkthrough: S here is Sunday, the usual crossword abbreviation behind 'Sun'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spurge is a family of plants, Euphorbia, with milky sap, many of them herbaceous.

clue.text: Learner, one with quite distinctive uniform

parts.note: L is a learner, from the British L-plate on learner drivers' cars
I is the Roman numeral for one
very and quite both intensify, as in very good

explanation.surface: A trainee in a rather unusual outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: Livery is the special uniform worn by servants or members of a guild, or a company's colour scheme.

clue.text: Guest is missing it as coverage for viewers?

indicators.note: is missing means lacks, so the named letters are taken away

parts.note: a visitor is a guest

explanation.surface: A TV guest misses a programme the audience is watching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'viewers' suggests a TV audience, but it means eyes, which a visor shades.
explanation.definitionFit: A visor shields the eyes, so it covers what one sees with.

clue.text: Popular Australian film about chap losing money getting fearful

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: about means around, so the film's letters enclose the other piece

parts.note: pic is short for picture, a film

indicators.note: losing means a letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a man is a chap

explanation.surface: A hit Australian movie about a broke man who becomes frightened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular' is IN as in fashionable, not a hit film; the film is just PIC, a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in a panic is gripped by sudden fear and alarm.

clue.text: Turn up part of final page in proposal

indicators.note: Turn up says the hidden letters are read backwards
part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone finds a scheme tucked away on the last page of a document.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft defined 'in proposal', but 'in' is a link word joining wordplay to definition; a plan is a proposal, not 'in proposal'. 'Turn up' suits a down clue, read bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan is a scheme or suggestion put forward for consideration.

clue.text: Most of class to be arranged for part of a challenging course?

indicators.note: arranged means set out in a new order, so the letters are reordered
most of means all but the last letter

explanation.surface: Most of a class is being organised for an assault course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' drops the last S from CLASS; 'arranged' reorders CLAS plus TOBE.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle course has hurdles and barriers, each one an obstacle to overcome.

clue.text: Reportedly, hold up decoration on a wall

indicators.note: reportedly means as spoken or heard, signalling a word that sounds like another

parts.note: to freeze is to halt or stop, to hold up progress

explanation.surface: Word is that a painted wall-border was stolen in a robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hold up' suggests a robbery, but it means stop, as in freezing an action.
explanation.definitionFit: A frieze is a decorated horizontal band along the top of a wall.

clue.text: Musician goes round narrow beam of light that's out of place?

indicators.note: goes round means encircles, so the musician's name encloses the other piece

parts.note: Sting is the English rock musician, formerly of the Police
a ray is a thin beam of light

explanation.surface: A rock star caught in a spotlight that has wandered off its mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Straying means wandering away from where one belongs, hence being where one should not be.

clue.text: Educational achievement of French and other EU nationality in short

parts.note: de is French for of

indicators.note: in short means abbreviated, dropping the last letter

parts.note: Greek is a nationality in the European Union, alongside French

explanation.surface: Qualifications held by French people and another European nationality, briefly.
explanation.definitionFit: A degree is a qualification awarded by a university on completing a course.
